questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) I would rather
(B) to take the earlier flight
(C) than wait
(D) for six hours at the airport.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Would rather' is followed by a bare infinitive, so 'to take' must be 'take'. The corrected sentence is: 'I would rather take the earlier flight than wait for six hours at the airport.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) Bread and butter
(B) are the only breakfast
(C) that the hostel canteen
(D) serves before six in the morning.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Bread and butter' functions here as a single item of food and therefore takes a singular verb, 'is'. The corrected sentence is: 'Bread and butter is the only breakfast that the hostel canteen serves before six in the morning.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) Myself Rakesh, and I shall be
(B) handling the vendor coordination
(C) for the upcoming
(D) product launch.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Myself Rakesh' is not acceptable English; a self-introduction should read 'I am Rakesh'. The corrected sentence is: 'I am Rakesh, and I shall be handling the vendor coordination for the upcoming product launch.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) In spite of he worked
(B) through the night,
(C) the module could not be stabilised
(D) in time for the release.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'In spite of' is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or gerund, so 'he worked' must be 'his working' or 'the fact that he worked'. The corrected sentence is: 'In spite of his working through the night, the module could not be stabilised in time for the release.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The professor asked us
(B) whether we
(C) have read
(D) the paper he had circulated.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. After the past reporting verb 'asked', the present perfect becomes the past perfect, so 'have read' must be 'had read'. The corrected sentence is: 'The professor asked us whether we had read the paper he had circulated.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) He has been working
(B) in this organisation
(C) for the last March,
(D) handling vendor negotiations.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Since' is used with a point in time and 'for' with a duration, so 'for the last March' must be 'since last March'. The corrected sentence is: 'He has been working in this organisation since last March, handling vendor negotiations.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) Anyone who wishes to attend the workshop
(B) should register online
(C) and bring
(D) their identity card to the venue.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Anyone' is a singular indefinite pronoun, so formal usage requires 'his or her identity card'. The corrected sentence is: 'Anyone who wishes to attend the workshop should register online and bring his or her identity card to the venue.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) He complimented the team
(B) on the design,
(C) noting that the colours
(D) complimented the brand identity perfectly.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. Something that completes or matches another thing 'complements' it; 'compliment' means to praise. The corrected sentence is: 'He complimented the team on the design, noting that the colours complemented the brand identity perfectly.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) She is responsible for designing the circuit,
(B) testing the prototype
(C) and for the documentation of the results
(D) before the design review.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The series should keep the same gerund pattern, so the third item must be 'documenting the results'. The corrected sentence is: 'She is responsible for designing the circuit, testing the prototype and documenting the results before the design review.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) She speaks English
(B) like a native speaker does,
(C) which helped her
(D) during the client interaction.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Like' introduces a noun phrase, while a clause with a verb requires 'as'. The corrected sentence is: 'She speaks English as a native speaker does, which helped her during the client interaction.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) He is one of those managers
(B) who insists
(C) on reviewing every line
(D) of the final proposal.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. In the pattern 'one of those managers who', the relative pronoun refers to the plural 'managers', so the verb must be 'insist'. The corrected sentence is: 'He is one of those managers who insist on reviewing every line of the final proposal.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The air in
(B) the workshop smelled
(C) strangely
(D) when the ventilation system stopped working.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. After the linking verb 'smelled', an adjective is required, so 'strangely' must be 'strange'. The corrected sentence is: 'The air in the workshop smelled strange when the ventilation system stopped working.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Neither the supervisor nor the operators were aware
(B) that the sensor had been replaced the previous week,
(C) and the log book carried no entry about it.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer plural subject 'operators', and the past perfect correctly marks the earlier action.

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) She is used to
(B) work under pressure,
(C) which is why the firm
(D) assigned her the critical module.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. In 'be used to' meaning 'be accustomed to', 'to' is a preposition and requires a gerund, so 'work' must be 'working'. The corrected sentence is: 'She is used to working under pressure, which is why the firm assigned her the critical module.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) She requested for a short extension
(B) because the data collection
(C) had taken longer
(D) than she had expected.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The verb 'request' is transitive and is not followed by 'for'. The corrected sentence is: 'She requested a short extension because the data collection had taken longer than she had expected.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) The vendor has been informed
(B) about the delay in payment,
(C) and the accounts team has assured
(D) that the amount will be credited on or before Friday positively.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The word 'positively' adds nothing and is not standard in formal writing; the sentence should end with 'on or before Friday'. The corrected sentence is: 'The vendor has been informed about the delay in payment, and the accounts team has assured us that the amount will be credited on or before Friday.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The trainee could not hardly
(B) follow the instructions
(C) given in the manual,
(D) so he asked his supervisor for help.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Hardly' is already negative, so combining it with 'could not' creates a double negative; it must be 'could hardly'. The corrected sentence is: 'The trainee could hardly follow the instructions given in the manual, so he asked his supervisor for help.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The trainer asked us to switch off our phones,
(B) to take notes
(C) and that we should ask questions
(D) at the end of the session.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The third item breaks the parallel series of infinitives and should be 'to ask questions'. The corrected sentence is: 'The trainer asked us to switch off our phones, to take notes and to ask questions at the end of the session.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) Neither of the solutions
(B) proposed by the vendors
(C) were acceptable,
(D) so the tender was cancelled.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Neither' is singular, so the verb must be 'was acceptable'. The corrected sentence is: 'Neither of the solutions proposed by the vendors was acceptable, so the tender was cancelled.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The interviewer asked the candidate
(B) where he had worked earlier
(C) and how long he had stayed there,
(D) but did not ask him what was his expected salary.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A reported question takes statement order, so the clause must read 'what his expected salary was'. The corrected sentence is: 'The interviewer asked the candidate where he had worked earlier and how long he had stayed there, but did not ask him what his expected salary was.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Although the budget was approved in April,
(B) the purchase order was raised in June
(C) and the equipment arrived in August,
(D) because of which the delay in the trial run.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The final clause has no verb and is therefore a fragment; it should read 'because of which the trial run was delayed'. The corrected sentence is: 'Although the budget was approved in April, the purchase order was raised in June and the equipment arrived in August, because of which the trial run was delayed.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The team leader asked Rohit and I
(B) to prepare the slides
(C) for the quarterly
(D) business review.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The pronoun is the object of 'asked', so the objective form 'me' is required instead of 'I'. The corrected sentence is: 'The team leader asked Rohit and me to prepare the slides for the quarterly business review.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) All suppliers must comply
(B) to the revised
(C) safety standards
(D) before the next inspection.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. The verb 'comply' is followed by 'with', so 'comply to' must be 'comply with'. The corrected sentence is: 'All suppliers must comply with the revised safety standards before the next inspection.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The client
(B) rejected the proposal
(C) which we had worked on it
(D) for nearly three weeks without a single break.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The relative pronoun already functions as the object, so the extra pronoun 'it' must be removed. The corrected sentence is: 'The client rejected the proposal which we had worked on for nearly three weeks without a single break.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) The period when the plant remained closed
(B) caused heavy losses,
(C) the reason of which
(D) the management has not explained till today.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The idiomatic phrase is 'the reason for which', and the present perfect with 'till today' should be 'so far'. The corrected sentence is: 'The period when the plant remained closed caused heavy losses, the reason for which the management has not explained so far.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The manager
(B) made the trainee
(C) to rewrite
(D) the test cases before the demo.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The causative verb 'make' is followed by a bare infinitive, so 'to rewrite' must be 'rewrite'. The corrected sentence is: 'The manager made the trainee rewrite the test cases before the demo.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) If water will be heated to one hundred degrees,
(B) it turns into steam
(C) at normal
(D) atmospheric pressure.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A zero conditional expressing a scientific fact uses the present tense in both clauses, so 'will be heated' must be 'is heated'. The corrected sentence is: 'If water is heated to one hundred degrees, it turns into steam at normal atmospheric pressure.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Between the two shortlisted designs,
(B) the jury preferred the one that used fewer moving parts,
(C) mainly because it promised lower maintenance costs over its lifetime.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. 'Between' is correct for two items, 'fewer' is used with the countable 'parts', and the comparison is complete.

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) He denied
(B) to have taken
(C) the spare access card
(D) from the reception desk.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Deny' takes a gerund rather than a to-infinitive, so 'to have taken' must be 'having taken'. The corrected sentence is: 'He denied having taken the spare access card from the reception desk.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) I have met
(B) the client
(C) yesterday
(D) to discuss the revised scope.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The present perfect cannot be used with a finished time expression; either 'met' with 'yesterday' or the present perfect without it is correct. The corrected sentence is: 'I met the client yesterday to discuss the revised scope.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) Despite of the heavy rain,
(B) the field engineers reached
(C) the substation
(D) well before the scheduled time.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Despite' is not followed by 'of'; the correct forms are 'despite the heavy rain' or 'in spite of the heavy rain'. The corrected sentence is: 'Despite the heavy rain, the field engineers reached the substation well before the scheduled time.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) If the shipment arrives on time,
(B) we will be able
(C) to complete the installation
(D) before the client visited the site.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The sentence refers to future time, so the past 'visited' is inconsistent; it must be 'visits'. The corrected sentence is: 'If the shipment arrives on time, we will be able to complete the installation before the client visits the site.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The professor
(B) told the students
(C) on Monday
(D) they would receive their results, which left everyone confused about the day.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The adverbial 'on Monday' is a squinting modifier that may attach to either verb; it should be placed unambiguously. The corrected sentence is: 'The professor told the students that they would receive their results on Monday, which left everyone confused about the day.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) The engineer which designed the fixture
(B) has been invited
(C) to present the idea
(D) at the annual technical meet.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Which' is not used for people; the relative pronoun must be 'who'. The corrected sentence is: 'The engineer who designed the fixture has been invited to present the idea at the annual technical meet.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The man who was waiting at the gate
(B) turned out to be
(C) an one-time colleague
(D) of our project manager.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'One-time' begins with the consonant sound /w/, so the article must be 'a one-time colleague'. The corrected sentence is: 'The man who was waiting at the gate turned out to be a one-time colleague of our project manager.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The new recruit
(B) took to the work
(C) like a fish to the water
(D) and was handling live tickets within a fortnight.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The fixed simile is 'like a fish to water', without the article before 'water'. The corrected sentence is: 'The new recruit took to the work like a fish to water and was handling live tickets within a fortnight.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) Students who wish to participate
(B) at the hackathon
(C) must form teams
(D) of not more than four members.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. One participates 'in' an event. The corrected sentence is: 'Students who wish to participate in the hackathon must form teams of not more than four members.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Each and every one of the modules
(B) was reviewed twice
(C) before the code
(D) was merged into the main branch.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Each and every one' is a wordy duplication; 'every one of the modules' conveys the meaning. The corrected sentence is: 'Every one of the modules was reviewed twice before the code was merged into the main branch.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The security team did not find
(B) any unauthorised device
(C) on the network,
(D) nor they reported any suspicious login attempt.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. After 'nor' the auxiliary must come before the subject, so the clause must read 'nor did they report'. The corrected sentence is: 'The security team did not find any unauthorised device on the network, nor did they report any suspicious login attempt.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) Each of the engineers
(B) have submitted
(C) the project report
(D) before the stated deadline.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Each' is a singular determiner, so it takes a singular verb; 'have submitted' must become 'has submitted'. The corrected sentence is: 'Each of the engineers has submitted the project report before the stated deadline.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) He has been working
(B) in this problem
(C) for the whole week
(D) without taking a single break.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. One works 'on' a problem, not 'in' it. The corrected sentence is: 'He has been working on this problem for the whole week without taking a single break.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The design is elegant
(B) and economical,
(C) whereas it is also
(D) easy to manufacture at scale.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Whereas' marks contrast, but the clause adds a similar positive point, so 'and' or 'besides' is required. The corrected sentence is: 'The design is elegant and economical, and it is also easy to manufacture at scale.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) The role requires analysing data,
(B) writing clear reports
(C) and to communicate
(D) with international clients.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. Items in a list must share the same grammatical form, so 'to communicate' must be 'communicating'. The corrected sentence is: 'The role requires analysing data, writing clear reports and communicating with international clients.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) We have been waiting
(B) for the vendor's confirmation
(C) from three weeks,
(D) but no reply has arrived.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. A period of time takes 'for', not 'from', so 'from three weeks' must be 'for three weeks'. The corrected sentence is: 'We have been waiting for the vendor's confirmation for three weeks, but no reply has arrived.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The supervisor distributed the samples
(B) to each of the trainees
(C) so that everyone had
(D) enough of material for the test.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. Before an uncountable noun without a determiner, 'enough' is used directly, so 'enough of material' must be 'enough material'. The corrected sentence is: 'The supervisor distributed the samples to each of the trainees so that everyone had enough material for the test.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) Lesser candidates applied this year
(B) for the summer internship,
(C) although the stipend
(D) had been increased substantially.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Candidates' is countable, so the comparative must be 'fewer candidates'. The corrected sentence is: 'Fewer candidates applied this year for the summer internship, although the stipend had been increased substantially.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) She is
(B) the honest officer
(C) who refused
(D) a bribe offered by the contractor.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Honest' begins with a vowel sound and the sentence describes her generally, so the indefinite article 'an honest officer' is required. The corrected sentence is: 'She is an honest officer who refused a bribe offered by the contractor.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The vendor neither delivered the components on time
(B) nor he informed
(C) the purchase team
(D) about the delay.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. After 'nor' the subject and verb are inverted or the structures are kept parallel; 'nor he informed' must be 'nor did he inform'. The corrected sentence is: 'The vendor neither delivered the components on time nor did he inform the purchase team about the delay.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The supervisor will be inspecting the line
(B) tomorrow morning
(C) as soon as the first shift
(D) will have started.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A clause introduced by 'as soon as' expresses future time with the present or present perfect, so 'will have started' must be 'has started'. The corrected sentence is: 'The supervisor will be inspecting the line tomorrow morning as soon as the first shift has started.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) One should always verify their sources
(B) before citing a study
(C) in a research paper
(D) submitted for publication.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The indefinite pronoun 'one' must be followed by 'one's' or 'his or her', not 'their'. The corrected sentence is: 'One should always verify one's sources before citing a study in a research paper submitted for publication.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Fewer attention
(B) has been paid
(C) to data quality
(D) than to model accuracy.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns; 'attention' is uncountable and requires 'less'. The corrected sentence is: 'Less attention has been paid to data quality than to model accuracy.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) When I reached the auditorium,
(B) the keynote speaker
(C) was speaking
(D) for almost an hour.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. A duration completed up to a past moment requires the past perfect continuous, so 'was speaking' must be 'had been speaking'. The corrected sentence is: 'When I reached the auditorium, the keynote speaker had been speaking for almost an hour.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The manager asked the team
(B) to take stocks of the situation
(C) before committing
(D) to a new delivery date.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. The idiom is 'take stock of the situation', with 'stock' in the singular. The corrected sentence is: 'The manager asked the team to take stock of the situation before committing to a new delivery date.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) The delegation visited
(B) the Netherlands
(C) and an European research centre
(D) working on fuel cells.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'European' begins with the consonant sound /j/, so the article must be 'a European research centre'. The corrected sentence is: 'The delegation visited the Netherlands and a European research centre working on fuel cells.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) Ten lakh rupees
(B) are a large sum
(C) for a start-up
(D) in its very first year.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. A sum of money treated as a single amount takes a singular verb, so 'are' must be 'is'. The corrected sentence is: 'Ten lakh rupees is a large sum for a start-up in its very first year.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) Each of the applicants was asked
(B) to bring an original copy of the degree certificate
(C) to the verification counter on the day of the interview.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The singular 'each' agrees with 'was asked', the article 'an original copy' is correct, and the prepositional phrases are idiomatic.

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) He may not able to attend
(B) the design review
(C) because he is travelling
(D) to the client's site.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The structure requires 'be' after the modal, so the phrase must be 'may not be able to attend'. The corrected sentence is: 'He may not be able to attend the design review because he is travelling to the client's site.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) From the sales figures
(B) the analyst inferred
(C) that demand was falling,
(D) although the report itself inferred no such thing.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A writer or document 'implies' something, whereas a reader 'infers' it, so the final clause must use 'implied'. The corrected sentence is: 'From the sales figures the analyst inferred that demand was falling, although the report itself implied no such thing.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) All the data
(B) collected during the survey
(C) has been anonymised
(D) and stored in a secure server.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Data' used in a technical report is normally treated as plural in formal writing, so 'has been anonymised' should be 'have been anonymised'. The corrected sentence is: 'All the data collected during the survey have been anonymised and stored in a secure server.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The candidate hardly
(B) spoke clear,
(C) and the panel
(D) asked him to repeat his answer.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. An adverb is required after the verb 'spoke', so 'clear' must be 'clearly'. The corrected sentence is: 'The candidate hardly spoke clearly, and the panel asked him to repeat his answer.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The sooner we close the defect list,
(B) the better it will be
(C) for the release,
(D) which is schedule for Friday.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A noun cannot function as a participle here; the correct passive form is 'scheduled for Friday'. The corrected sentence is: 'The sooner we close the defect list, the better it will be for the release, which is scheduled for Friday.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Not only the interns
(B) but also the team lead
(C) were asked
(D) to attend the review call.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. In the 'not only ... but also' pattern the verb agrees with the second subject, the singular 'team lead', so 'were asked' must be 'was asked'. The corrected sentence is: 'Not only the interns but also the team lead was asked to attend the review call.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The new interface is
(B) high intuitive
(C) and requires
(D) almost no training.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. An adverb is needed before the adjective 'intuitive', so 'high' must be 'highly'. The corrected sentence is: 'The new interface is highly intuitive and requires almost no training.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The laboratory, that was renovated last summer,
(B) now houses
(C) three additional
(D) test benches.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A non-defining clause set off by commas takes 'which', not 'that'. The corrected sentence is: 'The laboratory, which was renovated last summer, now houses three additional test benches.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) Every candidate must carry
(B) their own stationery
(C) and submit the admission slip
(D) at the verification counter.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Every candidate' is singular, so the possessive should be 'his or her' in formal written English. The corrected sentence is: 'Every candidate must carry his or her own stationery and submit the admission slip at the verification counter.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) The committee discussed about the proposal
(B) for nearly two hours
(C) before referring it
(D) to the technical sub-committee.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The verb 'discuss' is transitive and is not followed by 'about'. The corrected sentence is: 'The committee discussed the proposal for nearly two hours before referring it to the technical sub-committee.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The presentation was clear and well structured,
(B) the data were current
(C) and the recommendations were practical,
(D) making it one of the best review we have seen.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A superlative with 'one of the' requires a plural noun, so 'one of the best review' must be 'one of the best reviews'. The corrected sentence is: 'The presentation was clear and well structured, the data were current and the recommendations were practical, making it one of the best reviews we have seen.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) Although the equipment was imported last year,
(B) it has been lying idle in the store room
(C) because the operators have not yet been trained to use it.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The contrast clause, the present perfect continuous and the passive perfect are all correctly formed, and no conjunction is duplicated.

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) You had better
(B) to inform the client
(C) about the delay
(D) before he hears of it elsewhere.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Had better' is followed by a bare infinitive, so 'to inform' must be 'inform'. The corrected sentence is: 'You had better inform the client about the delay before he hears of it elsewhere.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The machine has been working
(B) well since it was serviced,
(C) though it still runs
(D) slight louder than before.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. An adverb is needed to modify 'louder', so 'slight' must be 'slightly'. The corrected sentence is: 'The machine has been working well since it was serviced, though it still runs slightly louder than before.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) If the sensor would have been calibrated,
(B) the readings
(C) would not have drifted
(D) during the final trial.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The 'if' clause of a third conditional takes the past perfect, not 'would have', so it must read 'If the sensor had been calibrated'. The corrected sentence is: 'If the sensor had been calibrated, the readings would not have drifted during the final trial.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The stationary ordered for the office
(B) arrived late,
(C) which delayed
(D) the printing of the annual report.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Stationary' means not moving; office supplies are 'stationery'. The corrected sentence is: 'The stationery ordered for the office arrived late, which delayed the printing of the annual report.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) He advice his juniors
(B) to document every change
(C) before pushing the code
(D) to the shared repository.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Advice' is a noun; the verb is 'advise'. The corrected sentence is: 'He advises his juniors to document every change before pushing the code to the shared repository.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) I shall look
(B) after the matter
(C) and revert to you
(D) by tomorrow evening.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Look after' means to take care of a person; to examine a matter, the correct phrasal verb is 'look into'. The corrected sentence is: 'I shall look into the matter and revert to you by tomorrow evening.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) She is knowing
(B) the answer to the question
(C) but refuses
(D) to share it with the group.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Know' is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous form, so 'is knowing' must be 'knows'. The corrected sentence is: 'She knows the answer to the question but refuses to share it with the group.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Between you and I,
(B) the revised proposal
(C) is far weaker
(D) than the one we submitted last year.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A pronoun after the preposition 'between' must be in the objective case, so 'I' must be 'me'. The corrected sentence is: 'Between you and me, the revised proposal is far weaker than the one we submitted last year.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The loose connection in the panel
(B) caused the machine
(C) to loose power
(D) during the demonstration.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Loose' is an adjective; the verb meaning 'to be deprived of' is 'lose'. The corrected sentence is: 'The loose connection in the panel caused the machine to lose power during the demonstration.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) No sooner had the server crashed
(B) than the support team
(C) has activated
(D) the backup instance.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The 'no sooner ... than' pattern with a past perfect main clause requires the simple past in the second clause, so 'has activated' must be 'activated'. The corrected sentence is: 'No sooner had the server crashed than the support team activated the backup instance.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The professor asked the students whether they had read the paper
(B) that had been circulated the previous week,
(C) and most of them admitted that they had not.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The reported yes/no question uses 'whether' with statement order, and the tenses are correctly backshifted.

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) If she had taken the aptitude test seriously,
(B) she would be working
(C) in a reputed firm
(D) since the last two years.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A period of time continuing up to now takes 'for', so 'since the last two years' must be 'for the last two years'. The corrected sentence is: 'If she had taken the aptitude test seriously, she would be working in a reputed firm for the last two years.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) She said to the team
(B) that the results were encouraging
(C) and that the next phase would begin soon,
(D) and told that the budget had been approved.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Told' requires a personal object, so the clause must read 'and added that the budget had been approved'. The corrected sentence is: 'She said to the team that the results were encouraging and that the next phase would begin soon, and added that the budget had been approved.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The board approved the proposal
(B) after an hour-long discussion
(C) on the historic rise
(D) in the sales of electric vehicles.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Historic' means memorable in history, whereas a rise studied over time is described as a 'historical' trend; here the intended word is 'historical'. The corrected sentence is: 'The board approved the proposal after an hour-long discussion on the historical rise in the sales of electric vehicles.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) If I was the project manager,
(B) I would reassign
(C) the two junior developers
(D) to the reporting module.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A hypothetical present situation takes the subjunctive 'were', so 'If I was' must be 'If I were'. The corrected sentence is: 'If I were the project manager, I would reassign the two junior developers to the reporting module.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Each of the three prototypes
(B) that were tested last week
(C) have a different battery capacity,
(D) according to the design log.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The head of the subject is 'each', which is singular; only the relative clause refers to the plural 'prototypes', so 'have' must be 'has'. The corrected sentence is: 'Each of the three prototypes that were tested last week has a different battery capacity, according to the design log.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The company
(B) had launched
(C) three new products
(D) in the current financial year.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. A period that is still continuing requires the present perfect, so 'had launched' must be 'has launched'. The corrected sentence is: 'The company has launched three new products in the current financial year.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The professor whom
(B) we thought
(C) was the chief guest
(D) actually arrived as an ordinary delegate.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The pronoun is the subject of 'was the chief guest', so the subjective form 'who' is required. The corrected sentence is: 'The professor who we thought was the chief guest actually arrived as an ordinary delegate.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Besides the technical round,
(B) candidates must also appear
(C) in a written test
(D) on quantitative aptitude.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. One appears 'for' an examination or test in standard usage. The corrected sentence is: 'Besides the technical round, candidates must also appear for a written test on quantitative aptitude.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Irregardless of the delay,
(B) the committee decided
(C) to proceed with the inauguration
(D) on the announced date.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Irregardless' is not a standard word; the correct form is 'regardless'. The corrected sentence is: 'Regardless of the delay, the committee decided to proceed with the inauguration on the announced date.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) Although the deadline was extended,
(B) but the team could not
(C) complete the integration testing
(D) before the client demonstration.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Although' and 'but' cannot be used together in the same sentence; one of them must be dropped. The corrected sentence is: 'Although the deadline was extended, the team could not complete the integration testing before the client demonstration.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The maintenance team arrived at six in the morning,
(B) replaced the worn bearings
(C) and tested the machine for an hour
(D) before handing it over, they left the site.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. Two independent clauses are joined only by a comma, creating a run-on; a full stop or a conjunction is needed. The corrected sentence is: 'The maintenance team arrived at six in the morning, replaced the worn bearings and tested the machine for an hour. Before handing it over, they cleared the site.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) This is to inform all employees
(B) that the office will remain closed on Friday
(C) on account of the maintenance work,
(D) and the same may be noted by everyone of you.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Everyone' cannot be followed by 'of you'; the correct form is 'every one of you'. The corrected sentence is: 'This is to inform all employees that the office will remain closed on Friday on account of the maintenance work, and the same may be noted by every one of you.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The supervisor let the operators
(B) to leave early
(C) because the maintenance work
(D) had been completed ahead of time.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Let' takes a bare infinitive, so 'to leave' must be 'leave'. The corrected sentence is: 'The supervisor let the operators leave early because the maintenance work had been completed ahead of time.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) He could not help
(B) to laugh
(C) when the robot repeated
(D) the same instruction for the third time.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Cannot help' is followed by a gerund, so 'to laugh' must be 'laughing'. The corrected sentence is: 'He could not help laughing when the robot repeated the same instruction for the third time.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) We shall
(B) discuss the matter
(C) in the detail
(D) when the complete data set becomes available.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The fixed expression is 'in detail' without an article. The corrected sentence is: 'We shall discuss the matter in detail when the complete data set becomes available.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) She suggested
(B) to postpone the sprint review
(C) until the client
(D) approved the revised scope.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund or a that-clause, never by a to-infinitive, so 'to postpone' must be 'postponing'. The corrected sentence is: 'She suggested postponing the sprint review until the client approved the revised scope.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) Each student and each teacher
(B) has been issued
(C) an identity card
(D) with their photograph printed on it.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The subject is singular, so the possessive must be 'his or her photograph'. The corrected sentence is: 'Each student and each teacher has been issued an identity card with his or her photograph printed on it.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Very less information
(B) was available about
(C) the vendor's financial position
(D) at the time of the audit.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Information' is uncountable, and the correct quantifier here is 'little', so 'very less information' must be 'very little information'. The corrected sentence is: 'Very little information was available about the vendor's financial position at the time of the audit.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) He will join the new project
(B) as soon as
(C) he completes the handover,
(D) and unless the client objects to it.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Unless' already means 'if not', so adding it after 'and' makes the clause contradictory; 'provided the client does not object' is the correct expression. The corrected sentence is: 'He will join the new project as soon as he completes the handover, provided the client does not object to it.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Her presentation was
(B) as good,
(C) if not better than,
(D) the one delivered by the keynote speaker.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. The first comparison must be completed, so the phrase should read 'as good as, if not better than'. The corrected sentence is: 'Her presentation was as good as, if not better than, the one delivered by the keynote speaker.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) Inspite of the rising costs,
(B) the company decided
(C) not to increase the price
(D) of its entry-level model.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The expression is written as two words, 'In spite of'. The corrected sentence is: 'In spite of the rising costs, the company decided not to increase the price of its entry-level model.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Many of the equipment
(B) in the testing laboratory
(C) needs recalibration
(D) before the next certification.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Equipment' is uncountable, so 'many of the equipment' must be 'much of the equipment'. The corrected sentence is: 'Much of the equipment in the testing laboratory needs recalibration before the next certification.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) He and myself
(B) have been nominated
(C) for the innovation award
(D) announced last week.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A reflexive pronoun cannot be used as the subject of a sentence, so 'myself' must be 'I'. The corrected sentence is: 'He and I have been nominated for the innovation award announced last week.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The workshop will cover version control,
(B) unit testing
(C) and how to deploy applications on the cloud,
(D) which the participants find most useful of all.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The relative clause compares 'most useful' without a complete comparison group and uses an awkward superlative; it should read 'which the participants find most useful'. The corrected sentence is: 'The workshop will cover version control, unit testing and cloud deployment, which the participants find most useful.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) The audit found that the records were incomplete,
(B) the approvals were missing
(C) and poor maintenance of the backup logs
(D) over the past two quarters.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The third item should be a clause like the first two, so it must read 'the backup logs were poorly maintained'. The corrected sentence is: 'The audit found that the records were incomplete, the approvals were missing and the backup logs were poorly maintained over the past two quarters.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The candidate answered
(B) most of the questions
(C) confident and clear,
(D) which impressed the panel.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. Adverbs are needed to describe how he answered, so the phrase must be 'confidently and clearly'. The corrected sentence is: 'The candidate answered most of the questions confidently and clearly, which impressed the panel.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The invoices are verified by the accounts section
(B) before payment is released,
(C) and the records are archived,
(D) so that any discrepancy can be trace later.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. After the modal and passive auxiliary the past participle is required, so 'can be trace' must be 'can be traced'. The corrected sentence is: 'The invoices are verified by the accounts section before payment is released, and the records are archived, so that any discrepancy can be traced later.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) The manager requested the interns to submit their reports
(B) by Friday afternoon so that the summary could be circulated
(C) before the review meeting scheduled for Monday.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The reported request uses 'requested + object + to-infinitive', and the purpose clause correctly takes 'could'.

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) Very few metals
(B) are so much useful
(C) as copper
(D) in everyday electrical applications.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Much' cannot modify an adjective in the 'so ... as' pattern, so 'so much useful' must be 'so useful'. The corrected sentence is: 'Very few metals are so useful as copper in everyday electrical applications.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) The committee insisted
(B) upon the chairman
(C) to resign
(D) within a week of the enquiry report.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Insist on' is followed by a gerund, not a to-infinitive, so 'to resign' must be 'resigning'. The corrected sentence is: 'The committee insisted upon the chairman resigning within a week of the enquiry report.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) He read the
(B) whole of the manual
(C) but understood only little
(D) of the section dealing with thermal limits.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Only little' is not idiomatic; the correct expression is 'only a little' or simply 'little'. The corrected sentence is: 'He read the whole of the manual but understood only a little of the section dealing with thermal limits.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) He left no stones unturned
(B) while preparing for the interview
(C) and finally secured
(D) a place in the core engineering team.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The idiom is 'leave no stone unturned', with 'stone' in the singular. The corrected sentence is: 'He left no stone unturned while preparing for the interview and finally secured a place in the core engineering team.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) As discussed in yesterday's meeting,
(B) the revised timeline has been uploaded
(C) to the shared drive,
(D) and the team is requested to go through the same and revert back at the earliest.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Revert' already means to reply or go back, so 'revert back' is redundant. The corrected sentence is: 'As discussed in yesterday's meeting, the revised timeline has been uploaded to the shared drive, and the team is requested to go through it and revert at the earliest.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The amount of visitors to the museum
(B) increased considerably
(C) after the renovation
(D) of the main gallery.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Visitors' is countable, so the correct noun is 'number of visitors'. The corrected sentence is: 'The number of visitors to the museum increased considerably after the renovation of the main gallery.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) Discussing about the design flaw
(B) took nearly an hour,
(C) after which the team
(D) agreed on a temporary workaround.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The verb 'discuss' does not take 'about', so the phrase must be 'Discussing the design flaw'. The corrected sentence is: 'Discussing the design flaw took nearly an hour, after which the team agreed on a temporary workaround.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) The defective batch was identified during inspection
(B) and was withdrawn from the warehouse,
(C) after which the supplier
(D) was asked to replacing the entire consignment.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. After 'asked to' the base form is required, so 'to replacing' must be 'to replace'. The corrected sentence is: 'The defective batch was identified during inspection and was withdrawn from the warehouse, after which the supplier was asked to replace the entire consignment.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) They reverted back to the earlier version
(B) of the firmware
(C) after the update caused
(D) repeated reboots on older devices.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Revert' means to go back, so 'reverted back' is redundant. The corrected sentence is: 'They reverted to the earlier version of the firmware after the update caused repeated reboots on older devices.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Badly damaged by the storm,
(B) the engineers inspected
(C) the transmission tower
(D) before authorising repairs.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The introductory participial phrase illogically describes the engineers instead of the tower. The corrected sentence is: 'The engineers inspected the transmission tower, which had been badly damaged by the storm, before authorising repairs.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) The students who
(B) attended the seminar
(C) said that it was more useful
(D) than them who skipped it expected.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A pronoun functioning as the subject of a clause must be in the subjective case, so 'them who' must be 'those who'. The corrected sentence is: 'The students who attended the seminar said that it was more useful than those who skipped it expected.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) He is more intelligent
(B) than any student
(C) in his class,
(D) which is why he was selected.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. Since he belongs to the class, the comparison must exclude him by using 'any other student'. The corrected sentence is: 'He is more intelligent than any other student in his class, which is why he was selected.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Neither of the two interns
(B) has completed
(C) their documentation
(D) before leaving for the holidays.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Neither' is singular, so the possessive must be 'his or her' to agree with it. The corrected sentence is: 'Neither of the two interns has completed his or her documentation before leaving for the holidays.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) I am living
(B) in Bengaluru
(C) since I joined
(D) the graduate trainee programme.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. With 'since' plus a past starting point the present perfect continuous is needed, so 'am living' must be 'have been living'. The corrected sentence is: 'I have been living in Bengaluru since I joined the graduate trainee programme.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) Because the network was unstable,
(B) so the video call
(C) was postponed
(D) to the following afternoon.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Because' and 'so' express the same relation and cannot be used together in one sentence. The corrected sentence is: 'Because the network was unstable, the video call was postponed to the following afternoon.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) We regret to inform you
(B) that your application has not been shortlisted
(C) for the current opening,
(D) and we wish you all the best for your future endeavours ahead.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. 'Future endeavours' and 'ahead' repeat the same idea, so 'ahead' must be deleted. The corrected sentence is: 'We regret to inform you that your application has not been shortlisted for the current opening, and we wish you all the best for your future endeavours.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Despite the repeated reminders of the client,
(B) the vendor failed to share
(C) the compliance documents
(D) before the audit began.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The idiomatic phrase is 'reminders from the client'; 'of the client' suggests the client was being reminded. The corrected sentence is: 'Despite the repeated reminders from the client, the vendor failed to share the compliance documents before the audit began.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) If the server fails again,
(B) the support team
(C) would escalate the issue
(D) to the infrastructure group.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. A real future possibility is a first conditional, so the main clause takes 'will escalate', not 'would escalate'. The corrected sentence is: 'If the server fails again, the support team will escalate the issue to the infrastructure group.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) Having been delayed by a signal failure,
(B) the passengers complained
(C) that the train
(D) reached the terminus two hours late.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The participial phrase describes the train, not the passengers, so the sentence must be rewritten to avoid the dangling modifier. The corrected sentence is: 'The passengers complained that the train, having been delayed by a signal failure, reached the terminus two hours late.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The report does not mention
(B) the cost overrun,
(C) the schedule slippage
(D) or neither the vendor's claim for compensation.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. In a negative series the items are joined by 'or', so 'or neither the vendor's claim' must be 'or the vendor's claim'. The corrected sentence is: 'The report does not mention the cost overrun, the schedule slippage or the vendor's claim for compensation.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) Of the two proposals,
(B) the committee selected
(C) the best one
(D) after a long discussion.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. When only two items are compared, the comparative degree is used, so 'the best one' must be 'the better one'. The corrected sentence is: 'Of the two proposals, the committee selected the better one after a long discussion.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The syllabus consists
(B) of six modules,
(C) each of which concludes
(D) in a practical assignment.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A module concludes 'with' something; 'conclude in' is not the correct collocation in this context. The corrected sentence is: 'The syllabus consists of six modules, each of which concludes with a practical assignment.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) We are
(B) looking forward to
(C) receive your confirmation
(D) so that the travel desk can book the tickets.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. In 'look forward to', the word 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund, so 'receive' must be 'receiving'. The corrected sentence is: 'We are looking forward to receiving your confirmation so that the travel desk can book the tickets.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) Much of the data collected during the pilot study
(B) was discarded because the calibration certificate had expired,
(C) but the remaining records were sufficient for a preliminary analysis.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. 'Much of the data' is treated as a singular mass here, and the causal clause with the past perfect is correctly constructed.

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) This year's revenue is
(B) higher than
(C) last year
(D) by nearly fourteen per cent.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The comparison should be with last year's revenue, not with the year itself. The corrected sentence is: 'This year's revenue is higher than last year's by nearly fourteen per cent.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) She was working on the dashboard
(B) the whole of yesterday
(C) and finally completes it
(D) late in the evening.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The narrative is in the past, so the present 'completes' breaks the sequence of tenses and must be 'completed'. The corrected sentence is: 'She was working on the dashboard the whole of yesterday and finally completed it late in the evening.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) The new safety protocol
(B) was prepared by the committee
(C) and was circulated to all units,
(D) but nobody has been followed it so far.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The clause mixes active and passive; it should read 'but nobody has followed it so far'. The corrected sentence is: 'The new safety protocol was prepared by the committee and was circulated to all units, but nobody has followed it so far.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) Every employee and every contractor
(B) were required
(C) to complete the safety induction
(D) before entering the plant.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. When two subjects are each preceded by 'every', the combination is treated as singular, so 'were required' must be 'was required'. The corrected sentence is: 'Every employee and every contractor was required to complete the safety induction before entering the plant.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) She plays the badminton
(B) every evening
(C) at the sports complex
(D) near her hostel.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. Names of games do not take the definite article, so 'the badminton' must be 'badminton'. The corrected sentence is: 'She plays badminton every evening at the sports complex near her hostel.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The manager assured the client
(B) that the data would be insured
(C) against accidental loss
(D) by a daily backup routine.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. Protection by a backup routine is 'ensured'; 'insured' refers to an insurance policy. The corrected sentence is: 'The manager assured the client that the data would be ensured against accidental loss by a daily backup routine.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) Had the client approved the design earlier,
(B) the team
(C) will have completed
(D) the fabrication by now.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. An unreal past condition takes 'would have completed' in the main clause. The corrected sentence is: 'Had the client approved the design earlier, the team would have completed the fabrication by now.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The two
(B) departments have been
(C) at logger heads over the budget,
(D) which has delayed the purchase of the new testing rig.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The idiomatic expression is 'at loggerheads', written as one word. The corrected sentence is: 'The two departments have been at loggerheads over the budget, which has delayed the purchase of the new testing rig.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The number of complaints received by the helpdesk
(B) has fallen steadily since the new ticketing system was introduced,
(C) although the volume of calls has remained the same.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. 'The number of' takes a singular verb, and the present perfect with 'since' is correctly used for a period continuing to the present.

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) He has joined the firm in 2021
(B) and has since handled
(C) several key accounts
(D) in the eastern region.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A definite past year requires the simple past, so 'has joined ... in 2021' must be 'joined ... in 2021'. The corrected sentence is: 'He joined the firm in 2021 and has since handled several key accounts in the eastern region.'

questions.questionText:
Find the part that should be corrected:

(A) He told the panel that
(B) he had worked
(C) on machine learning projects
(D) ever since he will graduate.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The clause describes a past starting point, so 'will graduate' must be 'graduated'. The corrected sentence is: 'He told the panel that he had worked on machine learning projects ever since he graduated.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) Being a rainy day,
(B) the site inspection
(C) was postponed
(D) to the first week of the next month.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. The participial phrase has no logical subject to modify, so the sentence should begin 'As it was a rainy day'. The corrected sentence is: 'As it was a rainy day, the site inspection was postponed to the first week of the next month.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) If I would have known about the schedule change,
(B) I would have informed
(C) the rest of the team
(D) well in advance.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Would have' cannot appear in the conditional clause; the past perfect 'had known' is required. The corrected sentence is: 'If I had known about the schedule change, I would have informed the rest of the team well in advance.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) Having finished
(B) the code review,
(C) the report was submitted
(D) by the senior developer within the stipulated time.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The participial phrase must modify the person who finished the review, so the main clause should begin with 'the senior developer'. The corrected sentence is: 'Having finished the code review, the senior developer submitted the report within the stipulated time.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The teacher advised him
(B) to read a newspaper daily
(C) and to listen
(D) to a radio in the morning.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. Media devices referred to generally take the definite article, so 'a radio' must be 'the radio'. The corrected sentence is: 'The teacher advised him to read a newspaper daily and to listen to the radio in the morning.'

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) We should plan in advance
(B) for the annual audit
(C) so that the documents
(D) are ready before the auditors arrive.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Plan' inherently refers to future action, so 'plan in advance' is tautologous. The corrected sentence is: 'We should plan for the annual audit so that the documents are ready before the auditors arrive.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) She almost answered
(B) every question in the test
(C) correctly,
(D) which surprised her classmates.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. 'Almost' is misplaced before the verb; the intended meaning is that she answered almost every question correctly. The corrected sentence is: 'She answered almost every question in the test correctly, which surprised her classmates.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) By the time the auditor arrived,
(B) the accountant
(C) already left
(D) for the branch office.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, so 'already left' must be 'had already left'. The corrected sentence is: 'By the time the auditor arrived, the accountant had already left for the branch office.'

questions.questionText:
Which part of the sentence is grammatically incorrect?

(A) The list of approved vendors
(B) were displayed
(C) on the notice board
(D) outside the purchase office.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. The subject is 'the list', which is singular; the plural noun 'vendors' inside the prepositional phrase does not control the verb, so 'were' must be 'was'. The corrected sentence is: 'The list of approved vendors was displayed on the notice board outside the purchase office.'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) The error rate fell
(B) more sharply in March
(C) then in April,
(D) although the volume of data doubled.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The word indicating comparison is 'than'; 'then' refers to time. The corrected sentence is: 'The error rate fell more sharply in March than in April, although the volume of data doubled.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) Most of students
(B) in the batch
(C) have already registered
(D) for the online certification.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. When 'most of' is followed by a specific noun, the definite article is required: 'most of the students'. The corrected sentence is: 'Most of the students in the batch have already registered for the online certification.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) They will finish the migration
(B) by Friday evening
(C) if nothing unexpected
(D) will go wrong.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. In a first conditional the 'if' clause uses the present tense, so 'will go wrong' must be 'goes wrong'. The corrected sentence is: 'They will finish the migration by Friday evening if nothing unexpected goes wrong.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) The start-up had to cut
(B) its coat according to the cloth,
(C) because investors had become cautious
(D) after the funding winter has set in.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The time clause refers to a completed past event, so 'has set in' must be 'had set in'. The corrected sentence is: 'The start-up had to cut its coat according to the cloth, because investors had become cautious after the funding winter had set in.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) Water is an essential resource,
(B) yet the city wastes
(C) nearly fifth of its supply
(D) every single day.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. A fraction used as a noun requires the indefinite article, so 'nearly fifth' must be 'nearly a fifth'. The corrected sentence is: 'Water is an essential resource, yet the city wastes nearly a fifth of its supply every single day.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) Each of the laptops issued to the trainees
(B) comes with a warranty
(C) and their own
(D) set of recovery media.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. The antecedent 'each' is singular, so 'their own' must be 'its own'. The corrected sentence is: 'Each of the laptops issued to the trainees comes with a warranty and its own set of recovery media.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) The report, which was prepared by an independent consultant,
(B) concludes that the plant can reduce its energy consumption by nearly a fifth
(C) without any major change in the production schedule.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The non-defining relative clause takes 'which', the singular subject agrees with 'concludes', and the fraction takes the indefinite article.

questions.questionText:
Which segment of the sentence needs correction?

(A) He prefers writing code in the morning
(B) to review documents
(C) in the afternoon,
(D) when the office is noisier.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. After 'prefer ... to', a gerund is required for parallelism, so 'to review' must be 'to reviewing'. The corrected sentence is: 'He prefers writing code in the morning to reviewing documents in the afternoon, when the office is noisier.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) The train
(B) leaves
(C) the junction
(D) before we will reach the platform.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. A clause beginning with 'before' refers to the future using the present tense, so 'will reach' must be 'reach'. The corrected sentence is: 'The train leaves the junction before we reach the platform.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) You could please forward
(B) the revised invoice
(C) to the accounts team
(D) before the end of the day.
questions.explanationText: Part A contains the error. A polite request uses 'could you' in question form or 'please forward' as an imperative; 'You could please forward' is not idiomatic. The corrected sentence is: 'Could you please forward the revised invoice to the accounts team before the end of the day?'

questions.questionText:
Choose the segment that contains the error:

(A) Neither of
(B) the two proposals
(C) were found
(D) suitable by the evaluation panel that met last Friday.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Neither' used as a pronoun is singular, so the verb must be 'was found'. The corrected sentence is: 'Neither of the two proposals was found suitable by the evaluation panel that met last Friday.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error:

(A) They got the air conditioner
(B) repair
(C) before the summer
(D) training programme began.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. In the causative 'get something done', the past participle is required, so 'repair' must be 'repaired'. The corrected sentence is: 'They got the air conditioner repaired before the summer training programme began.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the grammatically incorrect section of the sentence:

(A) A few of the sensors have failed,
(B) but most of them
(C) is still transmitting
(D) readings every ten seconds.
questions.explanationText: Part C contains the error. 'Most of them' refers to the plural 'sensors', so the verb must be 'are still transmitting'. The corrected sentence is: 'A few of the sensors have failed, but most of them are still transmitting readings every ten seconds.'

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) The committee has decided
(B) banning single-use plastic
(C) in all the canteens
(D) from the next academic session.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. 'Decide' is followed by a to-infinitive, so 'banning' must be 'to ban'. The corrected sentence is: 'The committee has decided to ban single-use plastic in all the canteens from the next academic session.'

questions.questionText:
Which part contains an error in usage?

(A) Not only did the team deliver the module ahead of schedule,
(B) but it also reduced the number of open defects by half,
(C) which the client acknowledged in a written appreciation.
(D) No error
questions.explanationText: All the given parts are grammatically correct, so there is no error. The 'not only ... but also' construction uses correct inversion in the first clause and parallel structure in the second.

questions.questionText:
Find the erroneous part of the sentence:

(A) She is the engineer
(B) whom the board believes
(C) will lead
(D) the new automation initiative.
questions.explanationText: Part B contains the error. The pronoun is the subject of 'will lead', so 'whom' must be replaced by 'who'. The corrected sentence is: 'She is the engineer who the board believes will lead the new automation initiative.'

questions.questionText:
Identify the incorrect portion of the sentence:

(A) A detailed feasibility study
(B) has been carried out by the consultants,
(C) and the findings have been shared,
(D) though no decision have taken yet.
questions.explanationText: Part D contains the error. The final clause needs a correct passive form, so 'no decision have taken yet' must be 'no decision has been taken yet'. The corrected sentence is: 'A detailed feasibility study has been carried out by the consultants, and the findings have been shared, though no decision has been taken yet.'

questions.questionText:
Select the part that contains the grammatical error:

(A) The two departments
(B) exchanged
(C) its data sets
(D) under a formal sharing agreement.
